User: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $15,000 in 1099 income (marketing, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,350 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
Assistant: Thanks — that’s a good amount of detail. Below I’ll (1) summarize which deductions you can take, (2) compare itemizing vs. the standard deduction for you, (3) show a short numeric illustration (actual vs. simplified home-office), (4) list the federal (and state) forms you’ll need, and (5) ask one quick clarification that changes the answer.

Short answer / overview
- You should almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2023 (Head of Household = $20,800). Your charitable gift ($1,350) alone is well under that.
- However, treat the 1099 income as self-employment income and claim business expenses (including a home-office deduction). Those business deductions reduce your self-employment profit (and self-employment tax) and can also affect your eligibility for the full student-loan interest deduction and your QBI deduction — so the home office deduction is likely beneficial.
- You can (and probably should) use the actual-method home-office deduction (Form 8829) rather than the simplified method in your case — it looks significantly better with the rent numbers you gave.
- Student loan interest is an “above-the-line” deduction (up to $2,500) but phases out starting at MAGI $75,000 (single/HOH). Whether you get the full $2,500 depends on your MAGI after self-employment adjustments.

Key things you can deduct / must report
- 1099 (self-employment) income: report on Schedule C. Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses related to that marketing work (the $1,350 if those are for the 1099 business).
- Home office: qualifies (exclusive use, 140 sq ft of 620 sq ft total). Two methods:
  - Actual method (Form 8829) — your share of rent, utilities, etc.; proportion = 140/620 ≈ 22.5806%.
  - Simplified method = $5 x 140 sq ft = $700.
  - With your rent ($2,400/month), the actual method gives a much larger deduction.
- Half of your self-employment tax is deductible on Schedule 1 (adjustment to income).
- Student loan interest: you paid $3,600 but the allowable federal deduction is capped at $2,500 and phases out with MAGI. If your MAGI (after half-SE tax adjustment) is under $75,000 you get the full $2,500.
- Interest income from Marcus and TD Ameritrade ($1,450 + $320 = $1,770) — report on Schedule B (required if total interest > $1,500).
- Charitable contribution of $1,350 — deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Because your standard deduction as HOH is $20,800, you will almost certainly take the standard deduction instead of itemizing unless you have a lot of other deductible items not listed here (mortgage interest, large state & local taxes up to $10k cap, significant medical expenses, etc.).
- Note: Unreimbursed employee expenses for W-2 work are not deductible for 2018–2025 under current law. If your $1,350 “work expenses” were for your W-2 job, they cannot be deducted. If they’re for your 1099 business, they can be.

Numerical illustration (estimates) — Actual home office vs. Simplified
Assumptions used: W-2 wages $64,800; 1099 gross $15,000; bank interest total $1,770; business expenses $1,350 (assumed for 1099 business); rent $2,400/mo (annual $28,800); home office 140/620 = 22.5806%.

A) Actual-method home-office
- Home office rent portion ≈ $28,800 * (140/620) ≈ $6,503
- Total business expenses = $6,503 (home office) + $1,350 = $7,853
- Net self-employment income ≈ $15,000 − $7,853 = $7,147
- Self-employment tax ≈ 15.3% × (0.9235 × 7,147) ≈ $1,010 → half deductible ≈ $505
- AGI before student interest ≈ 64,800 + 7,147 + 1,770 = 73,717 → minus half SE tax ≈ 73,212
- Since MAGI ≈ $73,212 (< $75,000), you should qualify for the full $2,500 student loan interest deduction (even though you paid $3,600).
- After student loan interest and standard deduction (HOH $20,800), taxable income is roughly in the $48k–50k range.
- You’ll also likely qualify for a Section 199A QBI deduction (~20% of qualified business income, roughly 20% of ~$7,147 ≈ $1,429), which further lowers taxable income.

B) Simplified-method home-office ($5/sq ft)
- Home office = $700; total business expenses = $700 + $1,350 = $2,050
- Net self-employment income ≈ $12,950
- Self-employment tax ≈ $1,830 → half deductible ≈ $915
- AGI before student interest ≈ 64,800 + 12,950 + 1,770 = 79,520 → minus half SE tax ≈ 78,605
- MAGI ≈ $78,605 (above $75k), so your student loan interest deduction is partially phased out — you would NOT get the full $2,500 (reduced to roughly ~$1,900 by the phaseout).
- Result: simplified method produces higher AGI and higher taxable income vs. the actual-method in your situation.

Bottom line from the numbers above: the actual-method home-office deduction is materially better for you (bigger business expense, lower AGI, full student loan interest deduction, and still get QBI). It also reduces SE tax because it reduces your net business income.

Forms and schedules you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040 (2023)
- Schedule 1 (additional income & adjustments) — student loan interest deduction and adjustments flow here
- Schedule B — if taxable interest > $1,500 (yes, $1,770)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report 1099 income and business expenses
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use actual-method home-office deduction (recommended here)
- Schedule SE — self-employment tax calculation
- Form 8995 (Qualified Business Income Deduction) — if you want to claim the simple QBI deduction (you’ll likely be under the threshold and can use the simpler Form 8995)
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (unlikely from details given)
- Keep your 1099-NEC (or 1099-MISC if applicable) and 1099-INT forms from your banks/brokers

State return
- Illinois Form IL-1040 — report federal AGI per state rules and any Illinois adjustments.

Records to keep
- Receipts for business expenses (the $1,350) and proof they are business-related.
- Home-office substantiation: floor-plan or notes showing square footage, lease/rent statements, utility bills if you plan to allocate utilities, and statement that the space is used exclusively for business.
- Receipts for charitable donations (you said you have the St. Mary’s receipt).
- Student loan interest statements (Form 1098-E from Navient or records of interest paid).

One important clarification that changes results
- Are the $1,350 “work expenses” business expenses related to the 1099 work (marketing) or are they unreimbursed expenses for your W-2 employment? If they are W-2 unreimbursed employee expenses, they are NOT deductible under current law (2018–2025). If they’re business expenses related to the 1099 income, you should deduct them on Schedule C.

Would you like me to:
- (A) prepare the rough tax calculation with exact numbers and give an estimate of federal tax and self-employment tax owed, or
- (B) draft the text you can paste into tax software for Schedule C / Form 8829 / Schedule SE, or
- (C) show the step-by-step entries you’ll need in typical tax software?

Tell me which you prefer and confirm whether the $1,350 expenses are for your 1099 work or your W-2 job.
